title: Relational Algebra and Joins
relevance: Tests whether candidates understand the procedural foundation of SQL—operators, composition, and join semantics that OAs and DBMS rounds probe with expression and join questions.

phases.goal: Establish what relational algebra is, its closure property, and the basic vs derived operator split.

must_hit.point: Relational algebra is a formal procedural query language: expressions specify not only what to retrieve but the order of operations (how).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says procedural / sequence of ops / dictates how, not only what.

must_hit.point: Closure: every operator takes one or two relations and returns a new relation, so outputs compose as inputs to later operators.
Basic operators are atomic (π, σ, ×, ∪, −, ρ); derived ones (⋈, ∩, ÷) are expressible via basics—e.g. X ∩ Y = X − (X − Y).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists basic vs derived and gives the intersection identity or equivalent.

must_hit.point: Projection π picks columns (vertical slice, duplicates removed); selection σ picks rows matching a condition (horizontal slice).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly maps π→columns and σ→rows; may note duplicate removal on π.

probes: What is relational algebra, and how do basic operators differ from derived ones?
What does the closure property buy you when writing expressions?

hints.1: Think about whether the language tells you only the result or also the steps.
hints.2: Name the six fundamental operators, then say which convenience ops are built from them.
hints.3: Procedural language with closure; basics are π σ × ∪ − ρ; derived include ⋈ ∩ ÷ with X ∩ Y = X − (X − Y).

phases.goal: Show how unary/binary operators, union-compatibility, division, rename, and join variants actually work.

must_hit.point: Cross product R1 × R2 pairs every tuple of R1 with every of R2: result has (m+n) columns and (X × Y) rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States column sum and row product rules for ×.

must_hit.point: Union/intersection/difference require union-compatibility: same degree (column count) and corresponding columns with the same domain.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both degree and domain/type alignment left-to-right.

must_hit.point: Division A(x,y) ÷ B(y) returns x-values in A paired with every y-value in B—used for “every”/“all” queries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links ÷ to universal quantification / Enrolled ÷ Course style.

must_hit.point: Rename ρ(T, R) is a query-only alias; disk schema unchanged; needed for self cross-product R × ρ(T, R).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says temporary alias / unchanged on disk / required for self-×.

must_hit.point: A join is conceptually cross product then selection; natural join matches on all common attributes and drops the duplicate column; equi join is a theta join using only =.
must_hit.evidence_hint: × then σ; natural on common attrs + drop dup; equi = equality condition.

must_hit.point: Inner joins drop unmatched rows; outer joins keep unmatched rows from left/right/both and pad missing side with NULL (full = left ∪ right outer).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts discard vs keep+NULL; names left/right/full.

probes: If R1 has m columns and X rows and R2 has n columns and Y rows, what is the shape of R1 × R2?
When are two relations union-compatible, and when do you need ρ?
How does a natural join differ from an equi join and from a left outer join?

hints.1: Start from Cartesian product size, then add the compatibility rules for set ops.
hints.2: Walk × → join-as-filter → natural vs equi → outer NULL padding.
hints.3: × gives (m+n) cols and X×Y rows; union-compat = same degree + same domains; join ≈ × then σ; outer keeps unmatched with NULL.

phases.goal: Contrast operator choices where semantics or convenience differ (basic/derived, set-difference order, inner vs outer).

must_hit.point: Derived operators are convenience only—they can be rewritten entirely with basic operators (e.g. intersection via double difference).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says derived = sugar / expressible from fundamentals.

must_hit.point: Set difference is not commutative: A − B ≠ B − A (tuples in A absent from B vs the reverse).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly says order matters / not commutative.

must_hit.point: Choose outer over inner when unmatched rows must appear: left keeps all left rows, right all right rows, full both—with NULLs on the missing side.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks join flavor by whether unmatched rows should survive.

probes: Why have derived operators if basics already suffice?
Why does A − B differ from B − A, and when would you pick a left outer join over an inner join?

hints.1: Ask what stays expressible if you only keep the six fundamentals.
hints.2: Separate rewrite-power (derived) from semantic order (difference) and row retention (outer).
hints.3: Derived = convenience (∩ = X−(X−Y)); difference order matters; outer keeps unmatched with NULL vs inner drops them.

phases.goal: Compose multi-step expressions: σ/π nesting, set ops on projections, and self-× with rename for comparative queries.

must_hit.point: π_Name(σ_Rollno=2(Student)) on Student(Rollno,Name,Age) selects the Rollno=2 row then projects Name, yielding B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Inner σ then outer π; final answer B.

must_hit.point: π_Name(Student) ∪ π_Name(Employee) needs projected Name columns for union-compatibility and yields distinct names {A, B, C, E}; π_Name(Student) − π_Name(Employee) yields {B, C}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Projects to one Name column first; union {A,B,C,E}; difference {B,C}.

must_hit.point: Female employees earning more than some male: Emp × ρ(Emp1, Emp), then σ on F/M and Emp.Salary > Emp1.Salary, then π Emp.Eid → {3, 5}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Self-× with ρ, gender/salary filter, project Eid; result {3, 5}.

must_hit.point: Self join for students in ≥ 2 courses: alias Study as T1,T2 with T1.S_id=T2.S_id and T1.C_id≠T2.C_id.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Same-table join via aliases; equal S_id, unequal C_id.

probes: Write the algebra for name of the student with Rollno 2.
Find names that are students but not employees, then female Emp.Eids earning more than at least one male.
How do you express “enrolled in at least two courses” with a self join?

hints.1: Compose inside-out: filter rows before projecting columns.
hints.2: For comparisons across rows of one table, introduce ρ (or SQL aliases) then ×/join and σ.
hints.3: π_Name(σ_Rollno=2(Student))→B; Student−Employee names→{B,C}; Emp×ρ(Emp1,Emp) with F>M salary filter→π Eid {3,5}.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Basics (π, σ, ×, ∪, −, ρ) are atomic; derived (⋈, ∩, ÷) are convenience rewrites—e.g. X ∩ Y = X − (X − Y)—so expressive power sits in the fundamentals.
Inner join drops non-matching rows; outer joins keep unmatched rows from left, right, or both and pad the other side with NULL (full outer = left outer ∪ right outer).
Set difference is not commutative: A − B keeps tuples in A absent from B; reversing operands changes the result.

gotchas.trap: Confusing projection with selection (which picks rows vs columns).
gotchas.correction: Mnemonic from the notes: Projection = columns; Selection = rows.

gotchas.trap: Treating set difference like union/intersection as order-independent.
gotchas.correction: Order matters: A − B ≠ B − A; A − B is tuples in A not in B (also A ∩ B′).

gotchas.trap: Assuming rename changes the stored relation.
gotchas.correction: ρ is a query-only alias; original data and schema on disk stay unchanged.
Relations must be union-compatible: same number of columns and corresponding columns with the same domain.

gotchas.trap: Expecting unmatched rows to survive an inner join.
gotchas.correction: Only outer joins keep unmatched rows (left/right/full), padding missing attributes with NULL.
